summary: Describes how initial MPPE session keys are derived from various credential types. It is meant to be a public reference for others who wish to interoperate with Microsoft products. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before locking messages you need a key. This explains how to make that key from things like a password, so other makers can match Microsoft's way.

questions: how to derive keys from ms-chap
subtitle: How to derive encryption keys from passwords for Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption

tldr.problem: When using Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE) to encrypt PPP connections, initial encryption keys must be derived from user credentials in a way that other systems can replicate for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents methods to derive MPPE session keys from MS-CHAP authentication credentials or TLS session keys, supporting 40-bit, 56-bit and 128-bit key lengths with specific cryptographic functions.
tldr.outcome: Provides an open reference for third-party implementations to interoperate with Microsoft products, though MPPE itself is described in RFC 3078.

facts.label: Key derivation basis
facts.value: Password hash or TLS master secret

today: RFC 3079 is an Informational RFC and provides the definition of MPPE key derivation methods. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the reference for implementations needing to interoperate with Microsoft products.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE) uses the RC4 algorithm to encrypt packets sent over PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) connections. The RFC explains how to derive the initial session keys from different types of credentials: passwords from MS-CHAP authentication, or session keys from TLS (Transport Layer Security) connections.

Session keys come in three strengths: 40-bit, 56-bit and 128-bit. MPPE session keys are changed frequently during a connection (possibly every packet), but the initial key must be set up from the user's credentials when the connection begins.
sections.eli5: When two computers lock messages during a connection, they need a secret number to start with. This RFC shows how to create that secret number from a password, in the exact same way Microsoft does it.

sections.title: MS-CHAP Key Derivation
sections.content:
MS-CHAP-1 is Microsoft's Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol. For 40-bit and 56-bit keys, MPPE uses the LAN Manager password hash. The first 8 octets of the LmPasswordHash result become the basis for the session key. For 128-bit keys, MPPE uses the Windows NT password hash (16 octets), hashes it again with MD4, then processes it through Get_Start_Key and Get_Key functions that use SHA-1 hashing.

The key derivation functions use two constant SHA pads (40 bytes each: one of zeros, one of 0xf2 bytes) and combine them with the password hash through SHA-1 to produce the final session key. Sample derivations in the RFC show the exact hexadecimal values at each step for passwords like 'clientPass'.
sections.eli5: The computer takes your password and runs it through special math functions multiple times, creating a locked version each time, until it has the right key for encrypting your data.

sections.title: MS-CHAP-2 Key Derivation
sections.content:
MS-CHAP-2 improves on MS-CHAP-1 by deriving separate send and receive keys. Both use the Windows NT password hash as the starting point. A GetMasterKey function combines the password hash hash with the NT-Response field from the authentication packet and a 27-byte magic constant through SHA-1 to produce a master key. The master key never encrypts data; instead, it feeds into GetAsymmetricStartKey which applies another round of SHA-1 with 84-byte magic constants (one for send, one for receive) to produce asymmetric send and receive keys. These are then processed by GetNewKeyFromSHA to create the final session keys.

The RFC includes sample 40-bit, 56-bit and 128-bit key derivations showing the exact challenge, response, and password values with their intermediate hashes at each step.
sections.eli5: MS-CHAP-2 makes two keys (one for sending, one for receiving) so the computer can check if data got changed. It uses the same password-to-key process but with extra magic numbers mixed in to keep them different.

sections.title: TLS Session Keys and Security
sections.content:
EAP-TLS is an authentication protocol that uses TLS to establish secure connections within PPP. MPPE can derive session keys from the TLS master secret instead of passwords. The TLS master secret acts as the master session key; asymmetric master session keys are derived from it using the algorithm in RFC 2716. Keys shorter than needed are padded with leading zeros; keys longer than needed are truncated. Asymmetric keys feed into GetNewKeyFromSHA to generate the final session keys.

For MS-CHAP credentials, security depends on password strength and changing passwords frequently, as 40-bit keys derived from the same password are always identical. For EAP-TLS, security depends on the strength of the TLS protocol and care in transmitting EAP-TLS master keys if the EAP server is on a separate machine from the PPP authenticator.
sections.eli5: Different ways to start the encryption (from passwords or from TLS) each have weak points. Passwords need to be strong and changed often; TLS needs proper network security when the authentication server is far away.

sections.title: Implementation and Coordination
sections.content:
The RFC references RFC 3078 which describes MPPE itself (negotiation, encryption method and key change algorithm). RFC 2433 and RFC 2759 document MS-CHAP and MS-CHAP-2. RFC 2716 describes EAP-TLS authentication. RFC 2284 covers EAP. RFC 2246 defines TLS 1.0.

The implementation note emphasizes that the initial session key in both directions is derived from the initiating peer's credentials and the first challenge, true for both unilateral and bilateral authentication and for each link in a multilink bundle. In multi-chassis multilink cases, implementations must ensure correct keys are generated on all participating machines.
sections.eli5: The RFC points to other RFCs that describe the full encryption process and the authentication methods. Different servers need to coordinate so they all use the same key.
